 Live .  6,483 viewing 6483 viewing Live page Updated 8 minutes ago Supreme Court rejects Trump's California ballot demands as Democrats rally on midterms eve
 Summary
 It's the final day of campaigning in the US midterms , where key elections will determine which party controls Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency - see how these elections could reshape US politics 
 The Supreme Court has rejected Trump's attempt to sideline thousands of ballots in California that he alleged may have been issued to non-American citizens - here's what you need to know 
 Elsewhere, millions of Americans have already voted, with a new midterm record set in Georgia, where a third of all registered voters have cast their ballots already
 The Democrats have high expectations heading into these pivotal elections, our North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher writes - but are the polls accurate? 
 Trump's Republican party currently controls both chambers of Congress - the Senate and the House of Representatives. Democrats are hoping to flip enough seats to win a majority
 What's up for grabs? All 435 seats in the House; 35 of the 100 seats in the Senate; and some state-level politicians, including governors - read our basic guide

 Democrats hoping for Texas upset published at 00:34 GMT 00:34 GMT 
 Image source, Getty Images Democrats are hoping for an upset in the Texas Senate race, especially because no Democrat has won a statewide election in the Lone Star state since 1988. 
 Democratic Texas state lawmaker James Talarico is facing off against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. Both candidates are holding rallies tonight in a last-minute effort to drum up more support. 
 The state launched the careers of the two Republican Bush presidencies - George HW Bush and his son George W Bush - but members of that same political dynasty have crossed the political aisle to support Talarico .
 Paxton became the Republican nominee after defeating Senator John Cornyn, a prolific fundraiser for the party. Paxton has been hit by several scandals, and was even impeached by the Republican-controlled Texas legislature. 
 Polls show an extremely tight race. And the two candidates are both scheduled to make one final appeal to Texas shortly.

 In border states with deep Canada ties, Trump’s tariffs are a factor published at 00:26 GMT 00:26 GMT 
 Jessica Murphy 
Canada digital editor 
 Image source, Reuters Image caption, Trucks approaching a US-Canada border crossing in British Columbia
 In a recent campaign ad, Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers sits at a bar and waxes lyrical about watching ice hockey while drinking Labatt - a beer with deep Canadian roots - saying: “here in Michigan we know Canada is not our enemy."
 "We need to end this tariff war now.” 
 That ad, by a Republican no less, is just one example of how the Canada-US trade dispute has been playing out in these midterm elections. 
 It's not a major issue in the race nationwide - though affordability is - but in some US states with deep ties to Canada, Donald Trump’s tariffs are a real factor. 
 Few states have deeper ties with Canada than Michigan. 
 Detroit sits across the river from Windsor, Ontario, a city with an auto sector that is deeply integrated with the US, but which is also currently tariffed. Polls also suggest that the Trump administration levies are broadly unpopular with Michiganders.
 With Rogers distancing himself from Trump on the issue, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has also been sharply critical, dismissing the dispute as "an insane tariff war we have no business fighting with Canada".

 Michigan just got (more) interesting published at 00:07 GMT 00:07 GMT 
 Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed (left) and Republican Mike Rogers have been fighting a tight race in the US state of Michigan
 As we await campaign rallies in Michigan , let's have a look at how this race is shaping up. 
 Republican Mike Rogers is taking on Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed in the normally Democratic-leaning state. 
 However, El-Sayed's campaign was a rocked yesterday when Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens endorsed Rogers .
 Stevens had previously offered her endorsement to El-Sayed after conceding defeat to him during a closely-fought primary contest in August.
 Throwing her support behind a Republican stunned many of her fellow party members, who condemned her decision to switch her support just two days before the election.
 Both Rogers and El-Sayed are holding competing rallies this evening. 
 Stick with us for more updates.

 Supreme Court throws out Trump's California ballot demands published at 23:51 GMT 2 November 23:51 GMT 2 November 
 David Willis 
Reporting from Los Angeles 
 Image source, Getty Images On the eve of the midterm elections, the US Supreme Court has rejected an attempt by the Trump administration to force the state of California to set aside thousands of ballots that it claims were sent to non-American citizens. 
 The US Justice Department had petitioned the court to order California election officials to set aside 20,000 mail-in ballots that the Trump administration believed may have voted illegally. 
 President Trump has repeatedly claimed that voter fraud is rampant and that Democrats steal elections by allowing immigrants to vote illegally. 
 Much of that he blames on mail-in or postal voting that is permitted in many Democratic states. Nearly 26 million people are registered to vote in California, and several lower courts had sided with election officials who argued the federal government was seeking to interfere in state elections and cast doubt on the outcomes. 
 California has 52 seats in the House of Representatives, more than any other state. Multiple studies and state audits have show that ineligible voting - including that perpetrated by noncitizens - is rare.

 A one-sentence rejection published at 23:32 GMT 2 November 23:32 GMT 2 November 
 The US Supreme Court did not give a reason for rejecting the Trump administration's request to sideline thousands of California ballots. 
 The decision was announced in a one-sentence order released by the court.
 "The application for injunction pending appeal presented to
Justice Kagan and by her referred to the Court is denied," it reads.
 The high court rejected the move by the US Justice Department hours after it filed a last ditch effort to segregate the disputed ballots on the eve of the midterm elections.

 What you need to know about Trump's request to sideline California ballots published at 23:18 GMT 2 November 23:18 GMT 2 November 
 Kayla Epstein 
US reporter 
 As we just reported, the US Supreme Court has rejected Trump's request to segregate California ballots on the eve of the US midterm elections. They moved with unusual haste, rejecting the Trump administration hours after it filed.
 After losing in lower courts, the Trump administration asked the US Supreme Court to intervene the day before the election in a highly unusual move.
 Here's the backstory: 
 Last month, the US justice department alleged that 20,000 "likely" noncitizen voters appear on California's voter rolls, and asked a federal judge to block those votes from being counted unless their citizenship was verified
 California officials pushed back against that tally, and argued that the Trump administration didn't have the authority to demand those votes not count
 Lower courts - including an appeals court, twice - ruled against the Trump administration
 The Supreme Court declining to hear the case means lower court rulings will stand, and essentially ends the Trump administration's emergency bid to disqualify the ballots

 Democrats are getting out the vote in Georgia published at 22:51 GMT 2 November 22:51 GMT 2 November 
 Carl Nasman 
Reporting from Georgia 
 Image caption, Cheryl, a volunteer for the Democratic Party
 Cheryl, a volunteer with the Democratic Party, tells me she's knocked on at least 1,000 doors since March in her quest to turn the state blue - the colour associated with her party. 
 And when potential voters open the door, they often have one man on their mind: Donald Trump. 
 It’s the president, Cheryl says, who is motivating people - even some independents and Republicans - to vote Democrat in Georgia. She says frustration is boiling over with the high cost of living. 
 Here in Roswell, a suburb north of Atlanta, Cheryl knocks on the door of Sally, a registered independent who says she is voting for all Democrats this year, because she wants politicians who will “stand up to Trump".
 Suburbs like this one in Georgia will be closely watched on Tuesday night for signs of how the state’s crucial races might go. 
 Image caption, Sally, who describes herself as an independent voter, says she is backing the Democratic Party in this year's midterm elections

 Iran war casts shadow over the midterms published at 22:39 GMT 2 November 22:39 GMT 2 November 
 Frank Gardner 
Security correspondent 
 Donald Trump’s war with Iran is now in its ninth month and as we just heard from the president , it still looms large over his tenure.
 In marked contrast to the previous US quick ‘in and out’ operations like last year’s Midnight Hammer air strike that targeted Iran’s nuclear sites, or last January’s decapitation of the Maduro government in Venezuela, this is starting to look like ‘a forever war’. 
 And forever wars are exactly what President Trump’s supporters expected him to avoid. Net result: oil, gasoline and diesel prices have shot upwards and stayed high, driving up inflation. 
 The low-intensity warzone that the Strait of Hormuz has become has constricted the global supply of vital commodities like fertilisers and Liquified Natural Gas. US bases up and down the Gulf and beyond have taken direct precision hits from Iran’s drones and missiles. 
 Separately, but not entirely unrelated, there is the Ukraine war, now grinding on in its fifth year. Trump’s apparent fondness for Vladimir Putin at the expense of Ukraine is not going down well with some in the US.
 It also baffles and irritates America’s allies in Europe. So the question is: what will change after the midterms if the Republicans lose control of Congress? 
 Remember that this president is one of the most unpredictable in history, so nothing can be ruled out.

 'It could happen!': Trump floats possible Iran deal on midterms eve published at 22:29 GMT 2 November 22:29 GMT 2 November 
 In the last couple of hours, both Donald Trump and his vice president have been speaking about the US-Iran war, which has sent oil prices soaring since it began in February.
 "Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible. It could happen!" Trump writes in a post on Truth Social, after claiming that "Oil Prices are DROPPING LIKE A ROCK". 
 Vance echoed that sentiment, telling reporters earlier in the day that he and the president "both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement".
 As a reminder: the price of fuel and its attendant cost of living concerns are among the topmost concerns for voters ahead of the midterm elections.

 Trump to appear on Fox News as part of his final campaign blitz published at 22:12 GMT 2 November 22:12 GMT 2 November 
 Image source, Reuters Image caption, Trump held a rally in Washington DC for Republican candidates on the day before the US midterm elections
 We've just heard from US President Donald Trump, who says in a Truth Social that he intends to appear on the Sean Hannity Show on Fox News tonight. 
 Trump's public schedule shows he is also participating in a host of virtual rallies for Republican candidates.
 The president says that he plans to appear on the Fox programme at 21:00 EST (02:00 GMT).

 In Florida, Cubans who voted for Trump feel blindsided by his immigration policies published at 21:49 GMT 2 November 21:49 GMT 2 November 
 Will Grant 
Reporting from Miami, Florida 
 Image caption, Ismael Labrador sits in his Miami office
 While reporting in Miami, there were a couple of striking things among the Cuban Americans I spoke to about deportations.
 The first was the acute sense among many Trump voters of having been deceived over the issue.
 Yes, they accepted that Trump spoke openly and often as a presidential candidate in 2024 about launching the “largest mass deportation in American history”. But some, like Cuban American immigration lawyer Ismael Labrador, still felt “blindsided” by the president. 
 “I wanted to get criminals out of the country,” the now repentant Trump voter told me. “But we never thought that he was going to go after everybody.”
 The other striking thing was the number of Cuban Americans who remain loyal to Trump on this divisive issue. Particularly among wealthier demographics, many people talked about these deportation policies as being “necessary” after years of softer measures under Biden.
 For the midterms, Florida will provide a fascinating referendum on the question among a group which voted overwhelmingly in favour of President Trump two years ago.
 Read more of my reporting from Florida and learn why some Cuban Americans are souring on the Republicans.

 Some Nebraska farmers say they feel betrayed by Trump published at 21:24 GMT 2 November 21:24 GMT 2 November 
 Sheila Flynn 
Reported from Nebraska 
 I arrived in Nebraska weeks before the midterms to talk to farmers and ranchers - a key demographic for Trump - about how they felt his administration was doing. 
 I wanted to discuss how the decision to import foreign beef had affected the cattle market and their bottom lines. As I spoke to locals in some of the top beef-producing counties, however, they explained how many other factors were also hitting them (and their wallets) incredibly hard. 
 The war in Iran and tariffs have made costs soar for their daily operations - everything from diesel to barbed wire to fertiliser. The cumulative effect, they said, has been devastating. 
 Farmer Don Batie and rancher Yvette Mannon say they feel betrayed - and believe many of their contemporaries will show that dissatisfaction at the ballot box. 
 Others in the industry, like Jake Wolfinger, were hesitant to place all the blame at the president’s feet. But they also didn't shy away from airing frustrations at Trump's perceived meddling in an industry they feel he knows nothing about. 
 Continue reading more of my reporting on American ranchers and how they’re wrestling with soaring costs - and their loyalty to Trump.

 In downtown Austin, Texas, the Democrats are excited published at 21:13 GMT 2 November 21:13 GMT 2 November 
 Gary O'Donoghue 
Chief North America correspondent, in Austin 
 They’re crammed into a small room at party HQ, spilling out onto the sidewalk, waiting to welcome Gina Hinojosa – the party’s candidate for Governor.
 Rosario Torres is a first time voter and a fashion student at the University of Texas. She tells me she’s one of the 7.7 million people who have already voted in Texas.
 “I really wanted to vote last year. I couldn't because I wasn't old enough. So now being able to vote and being able to be here, it's so exciting for me.”
 Fifty-year-old mechanic, Willie Lopez, says Hispanics in Texas are frightened to go out, scared that immigration agents will stop them. That’s why he’s voting Democrat right down the ticket.
 “Ninety percent of the people immigration stops - they're people going to work. Not like criminals, so yeah, we need to change.”

 What I heard on the ground in Texas published at 20:59 GMT 2 November 20:59 GMT 2 November 
 Gary O'Donoghue 
Chief North America correspondent 
 Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, An early voting queue in Texas
 A couple of weeks ago I travelled through Texas, from the Rio Grande Valley up to the countryside around San Antonio.
 What struck me most was the anxiety and unease among Republicans on the ground.
 In the Valley, Hispanic voters gave Donald Trump a huge boost in 2024.
 Many still back his border crackdown, but not the way ICE is detaining and deporting Latinos.
 Mario Guerrero voted for Donald Trump three times. This time, he tells me he's voting Democrat.
 Further north, in the new 35th district – drawn to be safe for Republicans but now rated a toss-up – I met rural Republicans worried about the price of gas. Several were unhappy with Ken Paxton as their party's pick for Senate.
 Jesse, a lifelong Republican, said he wasn’t sure if he’d vote for Paxton “I can’t believe I’m saying that’, he adds.
 Some conservatives won't vote at all.
 That may be the party’s biggest problem - as one young Republican volunteer put it to me, the midterms are "purely a game of turnout".

 What are the key states to watch for Senate? published at 20:47 GMT 2 November 20:47 GMT 2 November 
 Image source, Portland Press Herald via Getty Images Image caption, Susan Collins, who has held her seat in Maine for almost 30 years, faces close competition from Democrat Troy Jackson
 While 35 Senate seats are up for grabs, seven have been identified as crucial toss-ups that could go either way.
 Of these, six are currently held by Republicans and one by Democrats. 
 Republican state Alaska is considered by analysts to be one of the tightest in the midterms. The race features two candidates named Dan Sullivan (one Republican and one independent) - a similarity which sparked a lawsuit . 
 Iowa is traditionally a Republican stronghold, but Congresswoman Ashley Hinson is facing a tougher-than-expected challenge in her race against Democrat Josh Turek.
 Megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton is looking to become the first Democrat to win Kansas since 1932. Although the state was once considered reliably Republican, a recent CNN survey put Hamilton in front of incumbent Republican Senator Roger Marshall.
 In Maine , Republican Senator Susan Collins has been reelected continuously for roughly three decades. However, recent polling suggests Collins is neck-and-neck with her Democrat rival, Troy Jackson.
 In Michigan , a blue state, Republican Mike Rogers is taking on Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed. However, El-Sayed's campaign was a rocked yesterday when Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens endorsed Rogers .
 Jon Husted is defending his Ohio seat against a comeback bid by former Senator Sherrod Brown. Polls suggest the race is tight between Brown and Husted, who was appointed to JD Vance's seat last year after Vance became vice president. 
 Polls also suggest Democratic candidate James Talarico may be on the verge of turning a Texas senate seat blue for the first time since 1988. He is looking to beat the Republican Party's Ken Paxton . Stay with us for exclusive ground reporting from our correspondents who are spread across these toss-up states.

 Will Supreme Court intervene on Trump's California ballot demands? published at 20:38 GMT 2 November 20:38 GMT 2 November 
 David Willis 
Reporting from Los Angeles 
 Image source, AFP via Getty Images After two lower courts rejected a request by the Trump administration to set aside 20,000 ballots that it alleges may have been issued to non-American citizens in California, the US Justice Department is taking the matter to the Supreme Court.
 In a 22-page brief reviewed by the BBC, the Department maintains that ballots cast by non- citizens could "debase or dilute valid votes".
 On Friday, a federal appeals court declined the government’s request to segregate the ballots. 
 Election officials here have questioned the accuracy of the government’s claims, and have expressed concern that eligible voters could be disenfranchised. 
 They have also said that segregating ballots whilst voting is underway is infeasible. President Trump has repeatedly voiced opposition to mail-in voting, which got underway here in early October. 
 California is the most populous state in America with 23 million people on its voting register. CBS News – quoting figures from the California secretary of state’s office - reports that by Sunday night more than 6 million mail-in ballots had already been received. 
 Coming on the eve of the midterm elections it remains to be seen whether the Supreme Court will agree to the Justice Department’s request to intervene in the matter.

 How the AI data centre backlash is reshaping American politics published at 20:24 GMT 2 November 20:24 GMT 2 November 
 Kali Hays 
Reported on data centres across the US 
 Image source, Getty Images Image caption, An aerial view, a portion of the Meta Prometheus Campus, an AI data center and supercluster project, in Ohio
 Like my colleague just pointed out, rarely have I done reporting for a story in which essentially every person I spoke to about it mostly agrees. The backlash to data centres has turned into that sort of story.
 Simply put, no one seems to like them, regardless of political affiliation. And people are willing to fight to keep them away from the places they call home.
 Speaking this year about data centres with people from Oregon to Pennsylvania, I heard the same worries: utility bills rising, miles of farming land being bought up, the noise concern, and pollution.
 Then there is the inextricable link between data centres, technology billionaires, and artificial intelligence (AI). As the conversation about AI risks started this summer to leave tech circles and hit the mainstream, people I spoke to often wondered aloud why they would welcome such a massive physical intrusion that would in the end benefit AI. 
 Just because tech CEOs say they need it? So they can make more money on tech they keep saying may get us all killed?
 Those were not questions people found tough to answer.
